UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                    BEFORE THE
                      FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

Monongahela Power Company,

                        Complainant,

                 v.                                 Docket No. EL27-3-000

PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.,

                        Respondent.



     COMPLAINANT MONONGAHELA POWER’S ANSWER TO PJM’S MOTION TO
        DISMISS, AND MOTION FOR LEAVE TO ANSWER PJM’S ANSWER

         Complainant Monongahela Power Company (“Mon Power”) respectfully submits this (1)

answer, pursuant to Rule 213(a)(3) of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure,1 to

Respondent PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.’s (“PJM”) motion to dismiss; and (2) motion for leave

to answer PJM’s answer. 2 Mon Power reiterates its request that the Commission set this case for

settlement/hearing procedures including discovery that is needed to determine whether PJM acted

consistently with its filed rate.

         As set forth herein, PJM’s motion to dismiss wrongly contends that Mon Power’s claims

are barred by PJM Operating Agreement (“OA”) Schedule 1 section 1.8.2(d). That section covers

claims challenging a “selection, scheduling or dispatch of resources.” But PJM’s advance-

scheduling of gas generation is a “prescheduling” decision, not a “scheduling” decision, and




1
    18 C.F.R. § 385.213(a)(3).
2 PJM combined its motion to dismiss and answer into one pleading.
                                                           See Motion to Dismiss and
Answer of PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Docket No. EL27-3-000 (Oct. 26, 2026) (“PJM
MTD/Answer”).
 therefore is not within the scope of section 1.8.2(d). Specifically, OA Schedule 1 distinguishes

“scheduling” (which involves Day-ahead Energy Market and Real-time Energy Market processes)

from “prescheduling” (which occurs before the Day-ahead Energy Market), and PJM prior to this

litigation acknowledged that advance scheduling of resources in anticipation of a winter storm is

“pre-scheduling.”3

       The need for a complainant to be able to challenge advance scheduling is especially clear

on the facts here, where PJM undertook its advance scheduling in the name of reliability for the

entire PJM system, yet assigned its costs only to a subset of load (West Virginia customers).4 The

Commission should not allow the cost of maintaining PJM system reliability to fall only on

ratepayers in one state. Remedying that situation cannot fairly be construed as taking money from

non-West Virginia ratepayers; instead, it would allocate the costs of PJM’s system-reliability

actions the way they should have been allocated in the first place.

       PJM’s answer does not support deciding the Complaint on the existing papers rather than

setting it for settlement/hearing procedures including discovery. Among other things, PJM’s

answer mischaracterizes Mon Power’s claims as seeking to shift the burden of proof to PJM (when

in fact Mon Power has pleaded a prima facie case and seeks discovery of information from PJM

to use in proving that case), and raises disputes of fact (such as which factor or factors caused the

divergence of the locational marginal price (“LMP”) for Mon Power generation from the LMP for

Mon Power load) that underscore the need for discovery.




3
  See Complaint Exhibit No. MPC-0007 at 5 n.10 (discussing “Advanced Scheduled Resources
that are pre-scheduled to mitigate operational risk during cold and hot weather events, along with
gas holidays” (emphasis added)).
4 See Section II.A, infra.



                                                 2
          At bottom, Mon Power has alleged in detail, supported by two expert affidavits, that PJM

may have violated its tariff in a way that cost West Virginia ratepayers approximately $145

million. Settlement/hearing procedures including discovery are warranted before such a

substantial cost is left with those ratepayers, particularly given the affordability challenges they

already face.

I.       PJM’s MOTION TO DISMISS SHOULD BE DENIED

         The Commission should deny PJM’s motion to dismiss because it wrongly asserts that OA

Schedule 1 section 1.8.2(d) bars Mon Power’s claims. That section covers only PJM’s “selection,

scheduling or dispatch” decisions, which is to say, the Day-ahead Energy Market, Real-time

Energy Market, and manual dispatch processes. That section, however, does not cover PJM

decisions that took place before the Day-ahead Energy Market, such as the advance scheduling of

gas resources challenged by Mon Power’s Complaint here.

         A.     The PJM OA Does Not Bar Challenges To PJM’s “Prescheduling” Decisions

         OA Schedule 1 section 1.1 expressly identifies “three time-frames pertinent to the daily

operation of the PJM Interchange Energy Market: Prescheduling, Scheduling, and Dispatch.” 5

         Section 1.8.2(d), upon which PJM’s motion to dismiss relies, concerns “[s]cheduling[] and

[d]ispatch,” not “[p]rescheduling.” The surrounding provisions reinforce that temporal distinction:

         •      Section 1.9 addresses “Prescheduling,” meaning the pre-Day-ahead Energy
                Market actions that PJM may take to support reliability, including outage
                planning and emergency planning.6




5
    OA Schedule 1 § 1.1.
6 Id. § 1.9. See, e.g., id. §§ 1.9.1 (scheduling of generation and transmission outages); 1.9.9(f)

(“The Office of the Interconnection shall coordinate with other interconnected Control Area [sic.]
as necessary to manage, alleviate or end an Emergency.”).

                                                 3
           •      Section 1.10.1(a), by contrast, governs the later-in-time “scheduling processes to
                 implement a Day-ahead Energy Market and a Real-time Energy Market,” 7 and
                 section 1.10.1(d) specifies that “[s]cheduling encompasses the day-ahead and
                 hourly scheduling process, through which [PJM] determines [] a plan to serve the
                 hourly energy and reserve requirements of the Internal Market Buyers and the
                 purchase requests of the External Market Buyers.” 8 Similarly, provisions
                 including section 1.10.2 govern PJM’s “select[ion]” of resources based on market
                 offers, reliability needs, and operating characteristics. 9

          •      Section 1.11 governs “Real-Time Dispatch,” which occurs even after the Day-
                 ahead Energy Market and Real-time Energy Market. 10

          Thus, “selection, scheduling or dispatch” in section 1.8.2(d) refers to the operation of the

routine Day-ahead Energy Market and Real-time Energy Markets and manual real-time dispatch,

not the earlier-in-time reliability planning activities separately identified as “Prescheduling” under

section 1.9. Consistent with this understanding, PJM has described to the Commission advance

scheduling of gas generation resources in preparation for a winter storm like Winter Storm Fern

as “pre-scheduling.”11

          The reference to prescheduling authority within the 1.10 portion of the Schedule,

specifically in section 1.10.1(d), does not eliminate this distinction, but rather preserves it because

the section makes clear that such a decision is not part of “scheduling,” but rather is a

“condition”/exception to scheduling that occurs before “selection, scheduling or dispatch”

decisions are made by the Day-ahead Energy Market and Real-time Energy Market and PJM’s

real-time dispatch decisions. Specifically, section 1.10.1(d) provides in relevant part:



7 Id. § 1.10.1(a).

8 Id. § 1.10.1(d).

9 Id. § 1.10.2(a).

10
     Id. § 1.11 (emphasis added).
11 See Complaint Exhibit No. MPC-0007 at 5 n.10 (discussing “Advanced Scheduled Resources

that are pre-scheduled to mitigate operational risk during cold and hot weather events, along with
gas holidays” (emphasis added)).

                                                   4
         The following scheduling procedures and principles shall govern the commitment
        of resources to the Day-ahead Energy Market and the Real-time Energy Market
        over a period extending from one week to one hour prior to the real-time dispatch.
        Scheduling encompasses the day-ahead and hourly scheduling process, through
        which the Office of the Interconnection determines the Day-ahead Energy Market
        and determines, based on changing forecasts of conditions and actions by Market
        Participants and system constraints, a plan to serve the hourly energy and reserve
        requirements of the Internal Market Buyers and the purchase requests of the
        External Market Buyers in the least costly manner, subject to maintaining the
        reliability of the PJM Region. … Scheduling shall be conducted as specified in
        section 1.10.1A below subject to the following condition. If the Office of the
        Interconnection’s forecast for the next seven days projects a likelihood of
        Emergency conditions, the Office of the Interconnection may commit, for all or part
        of such seven day period, to the use of generation resources with notification or
        start-up times greater than one day as necessary in order to alleviate or mitigate
        such Emergency in accordance with the Market Sellers’ offers for such units for
        such periods and the specifications in the PJM Manuals. 12

        The five-day objection procedure in section 1.8.2(a), which uses the same phrase

“selection, scheduling or dispatch,” 13 confirms this distinction. That expedited procedure requires

participants to raise objections to discrete operational disputes relating to resource selection,

scheduling, or dispatch within five days of the relevant operating day. That process is not designed

to address challenges to a systematic advance-scheduling regime developed days beforehand and

based on information largely unavailable to market participants until weeks later (if at all).

        B.       The Commission’s PPL EnergyPlus Decision Does Not Support PJM’s
                 Interpretation Of PJM OA Section 1.8.2(d)

        PJM invokes PPL EnergyPlus, LLC v. PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 14 but that order

supports Mon Power. In PPL EnergyPlus, a generator claimed that PJM should have dispatched

particular units sooner during an emergency, but the Commission declined to reconstruct




12 OA Schedule 1 § 1.10.1(d) (emphasis added).

13 Id. § 1.8.2(a).

14 117 FERC ¶ 61,338 (2006) (cited at PJM MTD/Answer at 12, n.55, 14 n.64).



                                                 5
 alternative real-time dispatch and hypothetical market prices, citing section 1.8.2(d).15 The

Commission emphasized the “day-to-day stress of system operations” and the fact that real-time

dispatch decisions cannot be reversed, making it inappropriate to reconstruct hypothetical prices

based on different dispatch decisions.16

          Here, by contrast, Mon Power’s claim is about the advance scheduling that occurred well

before the day-ahead and real-time periods. Determining whether PJM’s advance-scheduling was

authorized does not require reconstructing hypothetical real-time dispatch decisions or market

prices, particularly because Mon Power’s requested remedy involves out-of-market uplift, not any

change to market prices or quantities.

          In PPL EnergyPlus, the Commission endorsed a similar claim as not prohibited by section

1.8.2(d). Specifically, the Commission rejected PJM’s argument that section 1.8.2(d) barred the

generator’s separate claim challenging application of an offer-price cap,17 explaining that section

1.8.2(d) does not bar “any issues that do not deal with the selection, scheduling or dispatch of

resources.”18

          C.     The Filed-Rate Doctrine Does Not Justify Dismissing Claims Seeking
                 Enforcement Of The Existing Tariff

          PJM relies on Old Dominion Electric Cooperative 19 to argue that the filed-rate doctrine

prohibits retroactive relief that would depart from the terms of the filed tariff, even where strict

application of those terms produces inequitable financial consequences. There, the tariff’s express

17 Id. P 35.

18 Id.

19 154 FERC ¶ 61,155 (2016), aff’d sub nom. Old Dominion Elec. Coop. v. FERC, 892 F.3d 1223

(D.C. Cir. 2018) (cited at PJM MTD/Answer at 13).

                                                 6
 $1,000/MWh offer cap barred reimbursement of costs above the cap; the utility sought an equitable

retroactive waiver despite conceding that the tariff prohibited payment.20 Mon Power seeks the

opposite: a ruling that PJM violated the existing tariff’s substantive limits. The filed-rate doctrine

forbids replacing a lawful rate with an equitable alternative, not enforcing provisions of the filed

rate that were violated. 21

          PJM also invokes 22 Oklahoma Gas & Electric Co. v. FERC 23            and Columbia Gas

Transmission Corp. v. FERC 24 to assert that the Commission cannot waive filed tariff requirements

or retroactively modify filed rates on equitable grounds. But those decisions prohibit retroactively

departing from the filed tariff; they do not address claims seeking a remedy for violation of the

filed tariff. Indeed, ISO New England Inc.25 recognizes an ISO’s obligation to correct prices

inconsistent with filed market rules. Although any remedy must comply with the tariff and

applicable statutory limitations, those remedial questions do not justify dismissal before Mon

Power’s allegations of tariff violations are adjudicated.

          PJM’s reliance on section 1.10.8(e)’s five-business-day deadline for correcting published

market results does not establish otherwise, for reasons similar to those discussed above regarding

section 1.8.2(a).26 That provision requires PJM to notify market participants of potential errors in

 published Day-ahead Energy Market or Real-time Energy Market prices or cleared quantities

within two business days and, if PJM determines corrections are necessary, to announce its intent

to post modified results by the fifth business day. By their terms, these deadlines govern PJM’s

identification and correction of errors in published market prices and cleared quantities, not the

filing of complaints alleging independent tariff violations involving facts that would not be

disclosed until well after the operating day.

          PJM also argues that, as a nonprofit, it cannot compensate Mon Power without shifting

costs to other market participants.27 But the need to identify parties lawfully responsible for any

corrective allocation does not transform Mon Power’s challenge of PJM’s advance-scheduling

practices into a “dispatch” dispute covered by section 1.8.2(d). Mon Power proposes, among other

alternatives, allocating the financial consequences of PJM’s system-wide reliability measures

among the loads they were intended to benefit, without undoing payments to generators or

rerunning the market.28 Whether such relief can be ordered consistent with the existing tariff, the

filed-rate doctrine, and applicable statutory limitations should be determined on a developed

record.

          Finally, PJM cites 29 Consolidated Edison Co. of N.Y., Inc. v. FERC, 30 Connecticut Valley

Electric Co. v. FERC, 31 and Towns of Concord v. FERC 32 for the proposition that FERC retains

discretion to deny retroactive relief even where a tariff violation has occurred. But those cases

(“Complaint”).

 address remedial discretion after the underlying violation has been considered; none establishes

that the possibility of denying relief requires dismissal before the facts have been developed.

       D.      PJM’s Power To Maintain Reliability Does Not Immunize PJM From
               Violations Of Its Tariff

       PJM’s remaining authorities establish an undisputed proposition: grid operators need

latitude to maintain reliability. Order No. 2000 33 and the Order No. 888 series of orders 34

recognized RTO responsibility for short-term reliability and emergency redispatch. But those

orders do not address prima facie allegations of a tariff violation by PJM.

       PJM OA Schedule 1 section 1.10.1(d) authorizes PJM to commit generation resources in

advance of an anticipated emergency only “as necessary in order to alleviate or mitigate such

Emergency”—a limitation PJM seeks to characterize as conferring broad operational discretion.

But PJM cannot convert that discretion into an exemption from the provision’s express conditions.

The statutory-interpretation decisions PJM cites 35 may support latitude in choosing among

authorized reliability measures, but none construes the PJM tariff or resolves whether the

challenged advance scheduling complied with it. The same distinction applies to Big Sandy Peaker

 Plant, LLC 36 and PJM’s other emergency-discretion authorities: the availability of reasonable

operational choices does not make practices that violate the tariff unreviewable. Moreover, the

challenged PJM advance scheduling at issue here was undertaken days before the relevant

operating days, rather than through split-second emergency dispatch decisions, which is the

context of PJM’s authorities.

II.    THE COMMISSION SHOULD GRANT LEAVE FOR MON POWER TO FILE
       ITS ANSWER TO PJM’S ANSWER

       Pursuant to Rule 213(a)(2) of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure,37 Mon

Power respectfully moves for leave to submit this answer in response to the answer portion of

PJM’s MTD/Answer. The Commission has discretion to accept an answer to an answer, and it

regularly does so where the answer assists its decision-making process.38 The Commission should

accept Mon Power’s answer because PJM’s answer raised new points to which Mon Power has

had no opportunity to respond. For example, PJM incorrectly asserted that “Mon Power attempts

to shift the burden of proof to PJM.” 39 In fact, Mon Power acknowledges that it bears the burden

of proof, and it seeks discovery to obtain the information it needs to sustain that burden. PJM’s

answer also introduces new factual material, including assertions about transmission outages on

Mon Power’s system that rest on records PJM did not attach. The Commission will benefit from

Mon Power’s responses to these and other points because they demonstrate that settlement/hearing

procedures including discovery are warranted.

37 18 C.F.R. § 385.213(a)(2).

38 See, e.g., Sierra Club; Nat. Res. Def. Council, Inc. & Sustainable FERC Project, 193 FERC

¶ 61,207, at P 13 (2025); Equitrans, L.P., 134 FERC ¶ 61,250, at P 6 (2011); Cal. Indep. Sys.

at P 20 (2008).

                                                10
           A.         PJM Concedes That It Undertook Advance Scheduling To Serve System
                     Reliability, But A Substantial Cost Was Allocated Uniquely To Mon Power
                     And West Virginia Ratepayers

          As an initial matter, it is crucial to highlight a point that PJM’s answer does not contest:

that PJM took its advance-scheduling actions to serve the reliability of the entire PJM system. One

significant cost of those actions—approximately $145 million resulting from the divergence in

LMPs between Mon Power’s generation and its load—was left for Mon Power and West Virginia

ratepayers alone to bear. That violates well-settled cost-causation principles embodied in the

Federal Power Act and the Good Utility Practice provision of PJM’s tariff, 40 and PJM does not

explain why the ratepayers of a single utility should bear the cost of a measure PJM undertook for

the benefit of the entire region.

          PJM’s answer repeatedly frames its conduct in system-wide terms. It describes Winter

Storm Fern as a “system-wide emergency,” 41 and it invokes the Department of Energy’s section

202(c) orders and the preparations of other RTOs to show that the storm was a serious emergency

across the region.42 PJM justifies its focus on gas-fired resources on grounds of system fuel

security and resource adequacy,43 casts its advance-scheduling regime as an “important reliability

tool for managing emergency conditions,”44 and warns that second-guessing such actions would

undermine the Commission’s ability to “safeguard the reliability of the grid.” 45 Nowhere does

41 PJM MTD/Answer at 3, 33 (emphasis added).

42

                                                  11
 PJM claim that its advance scheduling during Winter Storm Fern addressed a unique local need or

was undertaken for the particular benefit of West Virginia ratepayers.

          Measures taken to protect the whole system should be paid for by the whole system. That

is how PJM treated the other costs of its advance-scheduling regime: uplift paid to advance-

scheduled gas-fired resources was treated as eligible for broad allocation across the PJM region. 46

That sensible approach—that system-wide reliability should be procured by system-wide costs—

aligns with basic principles of fairness, which the tariff implements by providing that reliability-

related balancing Operating Reserve credits are allocated according to each market participant’s

share of real-time load across the PJM region. 47 The same concerns animate the cost-causation

principle, which provides that rates must “reflect to some degree the costs actually caused by the

customer who must pay them,” 48 and that a practice is unjust and unreasonable where there is “a

sizable gap between the benefits accrued by each LSE and the allocated cost.” 49

          The congestion and LMP-divergence costs of PJM’s system-reliability strategy, however,

were left on West Virginia ratepayers. PJM does not dispute this. It acknowledges that West

Virginia “ratepayers may have paid more while their generators earned less,” 50 and that Mon

Power’s generation units were “dispatched down due to congestion.”51

          PJM contends that Mon Power’s requested relief would come “at the expense of other

ratepayers in PJM’s region.” 52 But those are the very ratepayers on whose behalf PJM says it

acted. Having justified its advance-scheduling regime as providing a system-wide benefit, PJM

congestion costs.

         B.        PJM Mischaracterizes Mon Power’s Burden At The Pleading Stage

         In determining whether to set a complaint for settlement/hearing procedures, the

Commission asks whether a complainant pleaded a prima facie case.53 This requires a complaint

to meet both procedural54 and substantive 55 requirements. Once a complaint meets these

requirements, as is true here, the Commission should deny the motion and allow for

settlement/hearing procedures including discovery.56

         PJM characterizes Mon Power’s Complaint as “a fishing expedition” 57 and contends that

Mon Power fails to identify a tariff violation 58 and shifts the burden of proof to PJM. 59 Mon

Power’s Complaint does neither. Mon Power’s Complaint identifies the tariff violations, explains

each violation, and supports these allegations with evidentiary materials. Mon Power’s request

         Mon Power’s Complaint identifies and explains how PJM’s advance-scheduling practice

likely violated the PJM tariff. Mon Power alleges that PJM exceeded or misapplied its limited

(to be explored in discovery), PJM’s actions would violate this tariff provision.63

         A complaint must “provide the Commission with evidentiary materials, including

documents that support the facts in the complaint.” 64 The Commission, however, “does not require

a complainant to gather all factual evidence prior to a hearing.”65 The complaint must only raise

          C.      PJM Overstates The Complaint’s Reliance On The PJM Transmittal Letter

          PJM overstates the PJM November 2025 transmittal letter 74 as the “linchpin” of the

Complaint around which Mon Power “builds its entire case.” 75

advance schedule resources unless they are also committed in the Day-ahead Energy Market. 79 In

           D.      PJM’s Statistical Comparisons Of Gas And Coal Resources Are Irrelevant
                  And Fail To Refute Mon Power’s Undue Discrimination Claim

          PJM devotes a portion of its answer to system-wide market-share statistics, which PJM

contends show that coal resources saw a 73.7% increase in output during Winter Storm Fern

relative to 2025.87 From these aggregate figures, PJM concludes that Mon Power has no basis to

claim that PJM made unduly discriminatory or preferential dispatch decisions.88 But PJM’s

statistics answer a question Mon Power did not ask. The Complaint does not allege that PJM

refused to run coal generation during Winter Storm Fern; it alleges that Mon Power’s units were

available, did generate, but were often held at their economic minimum.89 Mon Power’s actual

claim is that PJM’s advance scheduling and commitment of natural gas resources, performed

outside of and in tension with the tariff’s least-cost market processes, committed more gas

generation than the market would have selected, distorting market outcomes and producing the

congestion and LMP separation that caused approximately $145 million in harm to Mon Power

and West Virginia ratepayers.90 PJM’s aggregate statistics do not respond to that claim.

          E.      That Transmission Facility Outages Were One Potential Cause Of The LMP
                  Divergence Does Not Negate That PJM’s Actions Were Another Material
                  Cause, Which Is A Fact-Laden Issue That Warrants Settlement/Hearing
                  Procedures Including Discovery

          PJM’s assertion that transmission outages on Mon Power’s own system were “the most

obvious and significant congestion driver” of the LMP divergence91 is unsupported and disregards

 the other apparent causes of the divergence. At most, PJM’s assertion raises a factual dispute

the relative contributions of the outages and its own advance scheduling. PJM’s only record

          Second, as Mr. Austria explains, there were three principal apparent causes of the LMP

divergence, most of which lie within PJM’s responsibility. 95 In order of appearance, the first cause

(meaning that PJM had a role in approving them), and one unplanned outage at Pruntytown. 98

 Outages like these are a fact of life in any transmission system, as PJM acknowledges.99         The

third cause is PJM’s advance scheduling of natural gas resources, a decision PJM alone made.100

LMP divergence. Mr. Hunger observed that the relevant outages existed before the severe LMP

divergence began, yet the system operated without material LMP divergence until January 24,

when PJM’s advance-scheduling actions took effect.101 Mr. Austria’s what-if case corroborates

which PJM approved in the case of Bedington and Black Oak) arguably lies within Mon Power’s

rejected an “unclean hands” defense where the respondents did not show that the complainants’

practice was a tariff violation. 105 It has also rejected the argument that other causes defeated

          F.     PJM’s Failure to Account for Building Closures Was a Known Forecasting
                 Error That PJM Cannot Escape By Pointing To Other RTOs Making A
                 Similar Error

          Mon Power alleges that PJM’s load forecast was materially overstated and resulted in the

advance scheduling of natural gas resources on an unjustified basis in violation of the tariff. 108

PJM’s advance-scheduling authority, if any, must be tied to necessity, and discovery is needed to

assess whether PJM complied with the tariff in exercising such authority.

          PJM made an undisputed error in its load forecasting by failing to include school, business,

and government closures in its forecasting assumptions, judged without any use of hindsight.109

& Elec. Co., 149 FERC ¶ 61,116, at P 87.

 In the post-COVID-19 era, “[i]ncreasing remote work has made closures more common,” 110 with

building closures being a natural consideration for the forecasts of any storm, not just major events.

Excluding business closures—roughly 2 to 3 GW of demand—in a forecasting methodology

cannot be condoned as a “good business practice” that would lead to the desired result “at a

reasonable cost,” as demonstrated by the loss of approximately $145 million to be paid by West

Virginia ratepayers.

        PJM cannot rely on forecasting errors made by other RTOs/ISOs or the Department of

Energy to justify its own mistake. It is well established that following an industry standard does

not, by itself, preclude liability associated with an action. 111

        PJM cites the FERC/NERC staff’s Winter 2026 Arctic Events Report, which states only as

a matter of fact that other RTOs/ISOs also over-forecasted load in anticipation of Winter Storm

Fern. 112 That report was not designed to analyze how badly any specific RTO forecasted load,

much less whether a specific RTO’s advance scheduling due to the forecasting error was justified.

        PJM also argues that the Complaint is a reflection of Mon Power’s own failed performance

in the market and that Mon Power could have conducted its own forecasting instead of relying on

a forecast from PJM. 113 But PJM is the entity responsible for managing any advance scheduling

of resources—based on what should be reasonably accurate forecasts.

(reasoning that “[A]spirational industry standards cannot suffice” to establish standard of care in
negligence).

(“Winter 2026 Arctic Events Report”).
113 PJM MTD/Answer at 31–32.

         Finally, PJM asserts that the “atypical” nature of Winter Storm Fern excuses its “larger

than typical” load forecasting errors.114 But the atypical nature of Winter Storm Fern does not

excuse PJM’s significant errors in forecasts, which excluded an obvious consideration that should

have been included no matter how severe Winter Storm Fern turned out to be. Further, PJM was

not bound by its forecast and could have “adjust[ed] resource commitments.” 115

        G.       PJM Conflates “Second-Guessing” Of Reasonable Operational Decisions
                 With Enforcing Tariff Compliance

        PJM downplays Mon Power’s Complaint as a utility seeking discovery simply because it

“[d]isagrees with its [b]ill.” 116 But Mon Power challenges PJM’s systematic advance scheduling

of gas-fired generation during Winter Storm Fern, which exacerbated congestion and imposed

approximately $145 million in losses on West Virginia ratepayers.           These decisions were

undertaken for system-wide reliability purposes, yet their financial consequences were

disproportionately borne by West Virginia ratepayers.         Nor is this a speculative “fishing

expedition.” The Complaint identifies specific tariff violations supported by contemporaneous

market data, expert analyses from Mr. Hunger and Mr. Austria, and PJM’s own descriptions of its

advance-scheduling practices. These allegations warrant targeted discovery into the necessity,

scope, and consequences of PJM’s actions.

        Good Utility Practice affords operational discretion among permissible alternatives; it does

not excuse violations of independent tariff requirements or preclude targeted discovery into

potential violations. Indeed, PJM’s own authorities confirm this distinction and support targeted




114 Id. at 32.

115 Winter 2026 Arctic Events Report at 14.

116 PJM MTD/Answer at 33.

 discovery into PJM’s conduct. Tenaska Clear Creek Wind, LLC v. Southwest Power Pool, Inc. 117

held that Good Utility Practice did not require SPP to select the least expensive engineering

alternative, but the proceeding followed FERC’s finding of discriminatory modeling practices

requiring a restudy.118 More significantly, Metzenbaum v. Columbia Gas Transmission Corp. 119

affirmatively undermines PJM’s position: there, the Commission expressly rejected an operator’s

hindsight defense, found the operator’s failure to respond to foreseeable winter conditions

imprudent notwithstanding its discretion and good faith, and disallowed nearly $2 million in

resulting emergency gas costs, plus interest (“unnecessary costs”).120        Far from prohibiting

regulatory scrutiny of emergency decisions, Metzenbaum demonstrates that the Commission may

examine their reasonableness based on contemporaneously available information and order

retrospective financial relief where warranted.

          Finally, the extraordinary financial stakes warrant expedited consideration. Mon Power

raised its concerns to PJM in March, sought information through July, and developed substantial

expert evidence before filing in October. The approximately $145 million at issue, consequences

for West Virginia ratepayers (underscored by the filings of the West Virginia Attorney General

and West Virginia Public Service Commission), and increased collateral obligations for Mon

Power distinguish this proceeding from ordinary billing disputes. Because critical unit-level and

      182 FERC ¶ 61,084, at P 41 (2023).
118 Id. P 1.

119 4 FERC ¶ 61,277, at 61,619–20, 61,623–24 (1978).

120 PJM’s remaining emergency discretion authorities likewise recognize operational flexibility,

not immunity from tariff compliance. See PJM MTD/Answer at 34 n.137 (collecting authorities).
Mon Power does not contend that every forecasting error or failure to select the cheapest
alternative violates the tariff. Rather, it seeks targeted discovery into whether PJM’s extraordinary
advance commitments satisfied the tariff’s necessity, nondiscrimination, and Good Utility Practice
requirements based on information available when the decisions were made.

 market-modeling information remains uniquely within PJM’s possession, expedited discovery

would facilitate prompt resolution rather than impede it. The Commission should grant fast-track

treatment under 18 C.F.R. § 385.206(b)(11) and (h), or alternatively expedite targeted discovery

and threshold proceedings.

       H.      Mon Power’s Proposed Targeted Remedy Does Not Seek To Re-Run The
               Market Or Alter Revenues Received By Generators

       PJM, 121 P3/EPSA, 122 and Vistra 123 mischaracterize or misunderstand the nature and the

timing of Mon Power’s requested relief. Each accuses Mon Power of requesting a “market re-

run,” 124 a remedy that Mon Power never requested.

       Mon Power agrees that rerunning the market is a disfavored remedy under Commission

precedent.125 As such, Mon Power has asked the Commission to determine, after discovery and a

full record, whether PJM violated or misapplied its tariff and, if so, what targeted remedy would

be necessary to correct the resulting consequences. Mon Power’s remedial theory includes treating

the financial consequences of PJM’s system-reliability actions as reliability-related costs that

should be spread across load on a load-share basis, which is consistent with PJM’s own reliability-

from” other consumers in PJM).
122 “P3/EPSA” are the PJM Power Providers Group and the Electric Power Supply Association.

123 “Vistra” refers to Vistra Corp. and Dynegy Marketing and Trade, L.L.C.

2026) (“Comments of P3/EPSA”) at 2; PJM MTD/Answer at 2.
125 Complaint at 53.

 related uplift framework and cost-causation principles.126 A targeted load-share remedy applied

to out-of-market uplift payments is not a request to rerun the market.127

          This system-wide cost sharing would likewise not “penalize generators or strip away make-

whole uplift payments,” as P3/EPSA wrongly claim.128 Mon Power’s requested remedy would

not affect the revenues received by generators—it merely asks that the burden of paying those

revenues be shared across the PJM region on a load-ratio basis instead of being assigned uniquely

to West Virginia ratepayers.

          The Commission has well-settled authority to correct improper cost allocations through

corresponding refunds and surcharges without rerunning the market. In Verso Corp., 129 the court

upheld refunds to customers who overpaid for reliability-related generation costs, funded by

surcharges on customers who underpaid. This reallocation did not constitute an impermissible

retroactive rate increase because the aggregate charge remained unchanged and was merely

distributed differently among ratepayers.130      Likewise, in Black Oak Energy, LLC v. PJM

Interconnection, L.L.C., 131 the Commission ordered PJM itself to pay refunds for improperly

allocated loss credits and authorized corresponding surcharges on other customers, expressly

observing that the adjustments would not change LMPs or require PJM to rerun the market.




126
      Id. at 39–40.
127 See Verso Corp. v. FERC, 898 F.3d 1, 11 (D.C. Cir. 2018) (holding that reallocating SSR costs

through surcharges was within FERC’s section 309 authority, and not a retroactive rate increase,
because “the aggregate rate remained the same, divided differently among the constituent payers”).
128
      Comments of P3/EPSA at 5; see also Vistra Protest at 6.
129 898 F.3d at 10–11.

        Here, Mon Power similarly seeks a targeted reallocation of reliability-related costs among

market participants, without altering market-clearing prices or payments to generators. Although

the precise remedy must be determined on a developed record, these precedents demonstrate that

retrospective, revenue-neutral cost reallocation is an established exercise of the Commission’s

remedial authority.

       Furthermore, section 309 of the FPA authorizes the Commission to perform “any and all

acts” and issue orders “necessary or appropriate” to carry out the FPA. 132 Courts have repeatedly

recognized that section 309 gives the Commission broad remedial authority, so long as the remedy

is consistent with the FPA and does not contravene its specific limitations.133 The available

remedies may include, for example, refunds, resettlement, reallocation, recoupment,

disgorgement, or other targeted relief that FERC deems necessary to remedy tariff violations or

unjust settlement consequences. Unlike section 206(b)’s refund-effective-date limitations for rates

found unjust or unreasonable, section 309 imposes no comparable limitation on remedies for

violations of an existing rate. 134 Here, Mon Power alleges that PJM violated its existing tariff—

133 See, e.g., Yaphank Fuel Cell Park, LLC, 189 FERC ¶ 61,121, at P 22 (2024) (explaining that

F.3d 354, 359 (D.C. Cir. 2017) (quoting Niagara Mohawk Power Corp. v. FPC, 379 F.2d 153,
158 (D.C. Cir. 1967)); Verso Corp., 898 F.3d at 10; Ameren Ill. Co. v. FERC, 58 F.4th 501, 503
(D.C. Cir. 2023) (explaining that section 309 of the FPA vests the Commission with broad
remedial power to perform any and all acts necessary or appropriate to carry out the FPA’s
statutory ends (quoting Consol. Edison Co. of N.Y. v. FERC, 347 F.3d 964, 967 (D.C. Cir. 2003)).
134
    See Pub. Utils. Comm’n of State of Cal. v. FERC, 462 F.3d 1027, 1048–49 (9th Cir. 2006)
(rejecting the Commission’s refusal to consider remedies for Tariff violations predating the refund

authority to order refunds for violations of an ISO’s filed tariff).

 not that the Commission should retroactively impose different tariff requirements. Accordingly,

the Complaint’s October filing date does not foreclose financial relief for the earlier violations.

       In view of the above, initial pleadings are not the appropriate time to litigate a precise

remedy. As the Complaint explains, discovery is needed to understand the details of PJM’s

advance scheduling and its impacts.135 The Commission recently affirmed this very point in Basin

Electric Power Cooperative, in which the Commission denied a motion to dismiss, refusing to

“deviate from its normal procedures for processing proceedings by dismissing them,” and stating

that it would consider “whether to exercise [its] discretion as to potential remedies, including

whether refunds could be warranted.”136 The same approach applies here. The Commission need

not decide at the pleading stage the exact form of relief, the precise allocation methodology, or the

amount of any remedy.137 Those questions should be tied to the actual facts developed through

discovery and resolved through settlement/hearing procedures.138 Dismissing the Complaint now

because the final remedy has not yet been selected would put the cart before the horse and deprive

the Commission of the record necessary to determine whether PJM’s conduct violated the tariff

and, if so, how the resulting harm should be remedied.


135 Complaint at 4, 34.

136 Basin Electric Power Coop., 195 FERC ¶ 61,189, at P 23–24 (2026) (emphasis added).

137 Similarly, in Valero Marketing & Supply Co. v. Longhorn Partners Pipeline, L.P., the
Commission denied dismissal as premature because the facts had not yet been developed and the
Commission could not properly evaluate either the alleged violation or “what the remedy should
be for such a violation.” 123 FERC ¶ 61,106, at P 24 (2008).
138 See S. Minn. Energy Coop. v. Interstate Power & Light Co., 197 FERC ¶ 61,085, at P 64 (2026)

(Commission will deny a motion to dismiss when “there is insufficient information in the record
to make a determination” as to justness and reasonableness under the FPA); La. Pub. Serv. Comm’n
v. Sys. Energy Res., Inc., 166 FERC ¶ 61,022, at PP 27–28 (2019) (denying motion to dismiss and
finding that the issues raised “cannot be resolved based upon the record before us and [] are more
appropriately addressed in the hearing and settlement procedures ordered below. Accordingly, we
set the Complaint for investigation and a trial-type evidentiary hearing under section 206 of the
FPA.”).

                                                 28
 III.   CONCLUSION

       The Commission should deny PJM’s motion to dismiss and set the Complaint for

settlement/hearing procedures including discovery.

        1.         I am the same Ricardo Austria who authored and signed on September 28, 2026,

an affidavit (“Opening Affidavit”) in support of Monongahela Power Company’s (“Mon Power”)

Complaint in this proceeding. I understand that my affidavit was designated Exhibit MPC-0019

to the Complaint.

        2.         I respectfully submit this reply affidavit in support of Mon Power’s answer and

motion for leave to answer the Answer of PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. (“PJM Answer”) dated

October 26, 2026. I do not offer legal opinions, including on whether PJM’s actions complied

with its tariff.

        3.         PJM is factually incorrect when it asserts—without a supporting factual affidavit—

that “the most significant factor” (PJM Answer at 27) causing LMP divergence between Mon

Power generation and load was transmission outages on Mon Power’s own transmission facilities,

and that Mon Power is “wrong on the facts” (id.) in suggesting that anything else contributed.
        4.      In fact, there were three apparent causes that contributed to the LMP divergence,

and the transmission outages, taken together, are only one of those three apparent causes. As my

Opening Affidavit (¶¶ 14-24) explained, the three apparent causes, listed in the chronological order

in which they first appeared, were:

    a. Baseline transmission constraints for west-to-east power transfers in the PJM grid. The
    Bedington-Black Oak Reactive Interface is the principal baseline transmission constraint,
    with the AP South Reactive Interface a second constraint. 1 PJM’s own planning study
    identified voltage collapse conditions and reactive power needs on this west-to-east transfer

       5.      Although I did not have access to PJM’s actual model or the data on gas generation

units upstream of the constraints that were advance scheduled, I created my own model and ran a

what-if case that strongly suggests that cause (c) was material. See Opening Affidavit ¶ 27. In

that what-if case, I approximated removal of cause (c) by modeling (1) fewer gas-fired units

committed or dispatched west (upstream) of the constraints and more resources east of the

constraints, in place of the advance-scheduled pattern; (2) the baseline transmission constraints in

the PJM grid; and (3) the outages of Mon Power transmission facilities that actually occurred. The

result was a materially smaller LMP divergence than was observed in the actual world in which

PJM did engage in advance scheduling of gas generation. The PJM Answer does not address my

finding.

       6.      Although I was able to approximate the impact of PJM’s conduct, the exact

contributions of each of the apparent causes discussed above can be determined only with PJM’s

actual model and data, which Mon Power seeks in discovery in this proceeding. PJM has not

provided the detailed information needed to determine the relative contribution of each cause, so

I did not assign percentage shares. What the record does show is that the LMP divergence became

severe when PJM’s advance scheduling was added to the baseline constraints and outages already

in place.

       8.      My finding from modeling of the what-if case is consistent with Mr. David

Hunger’s observation of the real-world data from a chronological perspective. Because baseline

transmission constraints in the PJM grid and the Mon Power transmission facility outages began

before the first operating day covered by PJM’s advance scheduling, Mr. Hunger was able to

compare the periods before and after that day. He observed that, although the relevant transmission

outages existed before the severe LMP divergence (which he calls “LMP separation”) began and

continued afterward, the system operated without material congestion impacts on LMPs until

January 24, 2026. He concluded that the preexisting transmission conditions set the stage for the

LMP divergence but do not fully explain its timing, severity, and persistence. See Hunger Aff. ¶¶

34-36, 40. The Pruntytown constraint shows the same pattern. Breaker B125 was out of service

from January 13, 2026, but the resulting “PRUNTYTO B122 CB” constraint did not bind from

January 18 through January 23, first bound on January 24, 2026, the first operating day covered

by PJM’s advance scheduling, and was still binding on February 8, 2026. PJM does not explain

its basis for saying that Mr. Hunger “tepidly” reached his conclusion (PJM Answer at 27), but in

any event factual discovery will, as explained above, enable the parties and the Commission to

determine more exactly the respective contributions of the three apparent causes of LMP

        10.     The PJM Answer also appears to suggest that Mon Power is wholly responsible for

the transmission outages of its facilities. In fact, it is commonplace for outages to be taken from

time to time to repair or to replace equipment. And PJM has a role in approving planned outages,

which it admits it exercised in the case of the Bedington and Black Oak outages discussed above.

See PJM Answer at 28.          Accordingly, those outages are best understood as within PJM’s

responsibility, not within Mon Power’s unique responsibility.

        11.     Regarding the other two apparent causes discussed above, PJM bears primary

responsibility. As the regional transmission planner, PJM is responsible for identifying baseline

constraints such as cause (a) and selecting solutions for them through its Regional Transmission

Expansion Plan (“RTEP”) process, and PJM itself has identified this condition in that process as

in need of improvement. Specifically, the PJM 2022 RTEP Window 3 study identified 2027/2028

baseline violations, including constraints on regional 500 kV transmission facilities due to high

levels of power imports into load centers, as well as inadequate reactive power support required to

                                                     6
 sustain reliable regional transfers. See n.2, supra. While this PJM study evaluated projected

system conditions for the 2027/2028 planning horizon rather than actual 2026 operating

conditions, the analysis was completed in 2023 and reflected trends that were already emerging at

that time. Since then, data center development and peak demand growth have continued to

accelerate. As a result, the underlying drivers behind the projected 2027/2028 reliability concerns

may have been present earlier than the study horizon suggests. PJM’s advance-scheduling

decisions were decisions exclusively made by PJM.

       12.     In conclusion, as a factual matter, PJM mischaracterizes the Mon Power

transmission facility outages as “the most significant factor” in causing the LMP divergence. The

record instead shows that the three apparent causes contributed together, and that the LMP

divergence became severe when PJM’s advance scheduling was added to the baseline constraints

and outages already in place. Discovery is needed to determine the exact contribution of each

apparent cause.
